questions.q: Silicon contains about 5 x 10^22 atoms per cm3. A polysilicon lot is certified at 9N (99.9999999%) total purity. Roughly how many impurity atoms per cm3 does that correspond to, and how does it compare with the ~1.3 x 10^15 cm-3 of boron a wafer maker adds on purpose for a 10 ohm-cm p-type substrate?
options: 5 x 10^16 cm-3, about 40 times more than the intentional doping
5 x 10^13 cm-3, about 25 times fewer than the intentional doping
5 x 10^10 cm-3, about 25,000 times fewer than the intentional doping
5 x 10^19 cm-3, roughly equal to the intentional doping
questions.explanation: 9N means 1 part per billion, so 5 x 10^22 x 10^-9 = 5 x 10^13 impurity atoms per cm3, about 25 times below the deliberate boron level of 1.3 x 10^15 cm-3; only a small fraction of those impurities are electrically active dopants.

questions.q: Why does the Siemens process go to such lengths (many-stage distillation, resin guard beds, complexing agents) to remove boron from trichlorosilane, when metals like iron receive comparatively little attention at that stage?
options: Boron trichloride is a solid at column temperatures and clogs the packing, while metal chlorides are volatile

Boron has a segregation coefficient of ~0.8 in silicon so crystal growth cannot reject it, and BCl3 boils only ~19 C below SiHCl3, making it hard to separate; iron (k ~ 10^-5) is rejected into the melt during crystal growth and FeCl3 is non-volatile anyway
Boron is the only impurity that survives the 1,100 C deposition step; all other impurities burn off as gases
Iron is removed earlier in the arc furnace by oxidative ladle refining, so none reaches the chlorosilane plant
questions.explanation: Boron goes almost entirely into the crystal during Czochralski or float-zone growth (k ~ 0.8), so it must be removed chemically, yet BCl3 (12.5 C) and SiHCl3 (31.8 C) have similar volatility. Metals segregate strongly to the melt and their chlorides stay in the column bottoms.

questions.q: A modern Siemens deposition reactor consumes 40-60 kWh per kg of silicon, and older ones 100-150 kWh/kg, even though the reaction SiHCl3 + H2 -> Si + 3HCl is only mildly endothermic. Where does most of the energy go?
options: Compressing hydrogen to the 5-6 bar operating pressure
Breaking the Si-Cl bonds, which are stronger than Si-O bonds
Thermal radiation from the ~1,100 C rods to the water-cooled bell-jar wall, which must stay cold so silicon does not deposit on it
Heating the slim rods from room temperature to 400 C at start-up, since cold silicon is nearly an insulator
questions.explanation: A grey body at 1,100 C radiates on the order of 140 kW per square meter, and the reactor wall is deliberately kept cold; rod count, pressure, reflective (silver-plated) walls and the FBR alternative all exist to reduce that radiative loss.

questions.q: The carbothermic reduction SiO2 + 2C -> Si + 2CO has an enthalpy of about +690 kJ per mole of silicon. Which statement about the submerged-arc furnace is correct?
options: The theoretical minimum is ~6.8 MWh per tonne of silicon and real furnaces use 11-13 MWh/t, so about 55-60% of the electricity goes into the reaction
Real furnaces use about 2 MWh/t because the reaction becomes exothermic above 1,800 C
The furnace is fuel-fired with natural gas because arcs cannot reach 2,000 C
Fine beach sand is preferred as feed because its high surface area speeds the reaction
questions.explanation: 690 kJ/mol divided by 28.09 g/mol gives 24.6 MJ/kg = 6.8 kWh/kg; the remainder of the 11-13 MWh/t covers heating the charge to ~2,000 C, melting, and heat carried out by CO gas. Lumpy quartz is required so gases can escape the packed bed.

questions.q: Why do the world's 300 mm wafer makers buy electronic-grade polysilicon almost entirely from Wacker, Hemlock, Tokuyama, OCI, and Mitsubishi Materials, even though Chinese producers such as Tongwei, GCL, and Daqo make roughly 95% of the world's polysilicon?
options: Chinese plants use the FBR silane route, which cannot reach better than 6N purity

Electronic grade requires 10-100x lower boron and phosphorus, etched and cleanroom-handled chunk, FZ test-ingot verification and 1-2 year customer qualification, and the whole EG market is only ~40-50 kt/yr, so incumbents with long-term contracts and traceable supply chains keep it
US export controls prohibit the import of any Chinese polysilicon for semiconductor use
Chinese polysilicon is sold only as granules, which cannot be loaded into a Czochralski crucible
questions.explanation: EG is a small (~3% of tonnage), slow-growing, qualification-locked market where purity, surface cleanliness, and traceability matter far more than price; Chinese producers have EG programs but as of ~2025 supply mainly 200 mm and domestic customers.

questions.q: A 300 mm Czochralski ingot has a 2 m cylindrical body grown at ~306 mm diameter. Using a silicon density of 2.33 g/cm3 and a per-wafer pitch of ~1.0-1.1 mm (775 um wafer plus kerf and polishing losses), which estimate is correct?
options: About 34 kg of body silicon and ~180 wafers
About 343 kg of body silicon and ~1,800-2,000 wafers, so roughly 0.2-0.25 kg of polysilicon per shipped wafer once the charge, crown, tail and pot scrap are counted
About 3,400 kg of body silicon and ~20,000 wafers
About 343 kg of body silicon and ~2,600 wafers, since kerf is negligible with diamond wire
questions.explanation: pi x (15.3 cm)^2 x 200 cm = ~147,000 cm3, times 2.33 g/cm3 = ~343 kg; a 2,000 mm body at ~1.05 mm pitch gives ~1,900 slices. With a ~400 kg charge and ~1,700 shipped wafers, that is ~0.23 kg polysilicon per wafer, of which only ~127 g is in the finished wafer.
